title: Habit stacking
header_line: My analysis of one book on habits. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: What do you already do every day that a new habit could ride on?
A student said: habit stacking is using other habits as the if-then, as the trigger and response.

I said the book's example is: after I put on my shoes, I immediately change into my workout clothes. My own: after I have my coffee, I grab my gym bag and get out the door, not get on a call and get distracted until noon and skip my workout.
I said you want a cue that has the same frequency as the habit you are developing: a cup of coffee every day is a consistent cue, so a daily workout can follow it.
A student said: I start the car to warm it up, and while it warms I let the dog out for the last time. It became part of the routine, and that is the only way I guaranteed it.
Another said: I leave an electrolyte powder next to my keys, so I see it before I start the car, make the drink and put it in the console. I had to do it intentionally, and now it is automatic.
I said: isn't it amazing, completely designing your external environment around triggers and cues, instead of letting the environment be designed by things you are not controlling?
What is the habit you already do every day, and what will you stack after it?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write a habit you do every day without fail.
Write a new habit you want.
Write the stack: after A, I will do B.
Write what you will leave next to your keys or door.
Write how you will know it has become automatic.

check.q: What is habit stacking, according to a student?
choices: Using one habit as the trigger for the next

check.q: What did I say the cue should match?
choices: The frequency of the new habit

check.q: What did I say to design instead of letting it be designed for you?

recap: Stack the new habit on one you already do. Design your surroundings.
